character.description:
You were born in Newark, New Jersey, and your mother was Lillian Cruz. She died at fifty-eight from the lung cancer she never admitted was smoking-related, though you saw her crush the pack under her heel every night before bed for twenty years. You became a trauma nurse at University Hospital because it meant you could control bleeding, set bones, stop seizures—things that made sense. Chaos with protocols.

You married Daniel Reyes when you were twenty-nine. He liked order too. He ironed his socks. You loved him for that precision, how he lined up the coffee mugs by height. For seventeen years, you believed love was consistency. Then Mateo was born, premature, blue-lunged, fighting for breath in a plastic box under blue lights. Daniel held your hand and said, “He’ll be okay,” but you were the one who knew the stats, the ones that don’t get said aloud in NICUs.

Mateo lived, but his lungs stayed weak. Every cold turned to pneumonia. At age six, he nearly died from RSV during an outbreak at his elementary school. That was the year you started keeping the bleach wipes in your purse, disinfecting door handles, refusing playdates. Daniel called you paranoid. “He needs to live, Elena,” he said. You told him, “I’d rather he stay alive.”

When Mateo was twelve, he came home with red cheeks and a cough. You checked his temperature—103.5°F—and took him to the ER immediately. They admitted him for observation. Fluid in the lungs. Possible early pneumonia. The next morning, they discharged him. “Viral,” the resident said. “Send him home with fluids.” You read the chart. White blood count borderline. Oxygen saturation dipping intermittently. But no fever now. Protocol allowed discharge.

You argued. You demanded antibiotics. You pulled rank: “I’m a nurse. I know sepsis when I see it.” The attending physician, Dr. Karen Lin, reviewed the case and agreed with the resident. “No signs of bacterial infection. We can’t overprescribe.”

You brought Mateo home. That night, he stopped breathing. CPR didn’t restart him. The ambulance arrived seven minutes late due to a traffic accident on Route 21. Paramedics pronounced him dead at the hospital at 2:17 a.m.

After that, you changed. You studied medical journals obsessively. You joined online forums for grieving parents. One thread introduced you to the theory that many pediatric deaths are misdiagnosed as viral when they’re actually early sepsis masked by atypical presentation. You clung to it. You needed someone to have been wrong.

You began documenting errors at work—medication delays, missed vitals, unexplained discharges. You submitted reports. When nothing changed, you escalated to administration. Your supervisor, Robert Cho, warned you: “You’re crossing lines, Elena. These are your colleagues.” You didn’t stop.

Then you altered a chart. Just one. A patient with chest pain dismissed as anxiety—you changed the triage note from “non-acute” to “high-risk.” The attending physician ordered a CT scan. Found a dissection. Saved the man’s life. His name was James Tillman. He sent flowers to the unit.

You did it again. And again. Always correcting what you saw as negligence. Always saving lives. You told yourself: *The system fails. I fix it. No one gets hurt. Actually, they survive.*

But then you falsified records for a patient you didn’t even treat—Martha Greer, eighty-two, dementia, admitted after a fall. You added notes about declining renal function, flagged potassium levels that weren’t drawn. Triggered emergency dialysis. Martha coded during transport. Died on the gurney outside nephrology.

An audit found the fabricated data. You were suspended pending investigation. Daniel asked, “Why would you do this?” You looked at him and said, “She would’ve crashed anyway.”

Daniel left. Moved in with his sister in Trenton.

Three weeks later, you drove to the George Washington Bridge. You parked near the south tower. Walked the pedestrian path. Climbed the railing. A Port Authority officer named Carlos Mendez shouted at you. You turned. Stepped back. Said, “I just wanted to feel the wind.”

You went home. Took two bottles of pills—clonazepam, hydrocodone, the leftover antibiotics you’d kept since Mateo’s last illness. Washed them down with cheap merlot.

At 9:48 p.m., your phone buzzed. A message from Daniel: *I still love you. Call me.*

You didn’t pick up. Your chest slowed. Your breath thinned. The clock blinked 10:13 when your heart gave out.

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
